title: Introduction: Reviewing 88 Videos and the Review Gate
text: Hi, I'm Sanjana, a project manager at Humanitarian's AI. Over the last 2 weeks of September, 88 fellow videos landed on my desk for review. This isn't a highlights reel. It's the record what I actually did, how I checked each one, and what made it through. Because reviewing isn't watching and clicking approve. Every video runs a gate first. Let me show you the gate and the 2 weeks it sorted. Here's the whole thing in one breath. It's easy to picture video review as hitting play and clicking approve. It isn't. Every one of these 88 videos went through the same three check

title: The Three-Check Gate: 4K Rendering, Branding, and GitHub Code The Scoreboard: Turning Review Logs into Honest Metrics with Claude
text: Gate before it reached a professor, and a lot of them bounced back first. So, here's the gate every video has to clear. Check one. Is it rendered in true 4K, both the wide cut and the vertical short, not just one? Check two. Is the branding right, the Humanitarian's AI handle, not a leftover Nick Bear Brown? Check three. Is the code on GitHub with the dimensions correct? Three passes, it's approved and goes to the professor. Any fail, it goes back to the fellow with an email saying exactly what to fix. 2 weeks of notes is a spreadsheet, not a picture. So, I did what I'd tell any fellow to do. I handed the raw tracker to Claude and asked it to turn the mess

Into a scoreboard. Not to judge anything, just to count it and lay it out honestly. And here's the scoreboard. 88 videos reviewed in 2 weeks from 22 different fellows. Of those, 78 cleared the gate and went up for approval. 10 came back needing fixes. And 71 already had their code on GitHub, where the work can actually be checked. That's the 2 weeks, counted honestly, the good and the sent back. Where did the 88 go? Not evenly. Almost half were Brutalist Toolkit videos, 41 of them, as that project scaled up. Madison was next at 18, then the AI plus one teams at 14. The rest spread thin across lyrical literacy, causal couture, the ramen effect, relocation engine, and walker. Eight projects, one reviewer. text: Gate doing its job on a good one. Jaynel's brutalist batch four videos, rendered in 4K, both cuts pass. Branding on the Humanitarian's AI handle, pass. Code on GitHub, pass. Three green. So, it's approved and uploaded straight to YouTube for the professors. No email, no back and forth. This is exactly what a clean submission looks like. But, most of the work is in the ones that fail. title: Clean Passes vs Returned Batches: How Feedback Loops Work Build Your Own Gate: Replacing Gut Calls with AI Checklists
text: For Harshitha's eight and Neelabs. That's the point of a gate, not to reject people, but to catch it, say exactly what's wrong, and let them fix it before a professor ever sees it. Your turn. If you review anyone's work or your own, build a gate instead of a gut call. Here's the prompt I'd run. Paste your log and have Claude turn it into a scoreboard and a checklist you apply to every item, the same way every time. Read what it hands back. The checklist is the real output. A good answer gives you three or four checks you can actually run. A vague one just says looks good, which is the gut call you're trying to replace. The review gate my two weeks at Humanitarian's AI with Sanjana Rao. Don't just watch the work. Run it through the gate. Thanks for watching.
